summary: Defines a content media feature schema for Internet fax, a way to describe the capabilities of a fax device and the features of a document. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Before sending a fax, you want to know what the other machine can handle. This is a standard way to write down those abilities.

questions: what is the internet fax feature schema
how do fax machines describe their capabilities
what is mrc in internet fax
subtitle: A shared vocabulary of feature tags that lets Internet fax machines say what resolution, color and image coding they can handle.

tldr.problem: Before sending a fax over the Internet, a sender needs to know what the receiving system can display or print, such as resolution, paper size, color and image coding.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists the media feature tags that extended Internet fax systems must recognize, in the syntax of the media feature set specification, and registers the fax-specific tags in its appendix.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that replaces and updates the schema in RFC 2531. It describes capabilities only and does not say how they are exchanged.

today: RFC 2879 is a Proposed Standard that replaces and updates RFC 2531, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 2879 defines a content media feature schema for Internet fax. It is a profile of the media feature registration mechanisms, meant for capability identification between extended Internet fax systems, which are systems that conform to the specification 'Extended Facsimile Using Internet Mail' (RFC 2532). It replaces and updates the schema defined in RFC 2531.

The media feature mechanisms do not define how capability information is carried; they only presume that it is transferred as text and give a textual format for describing it. The capabilities covered follow those of the TIFF file format for Internet fax (RFC 2301) and Group 3 facsimile. A companion document, RFC 2880, maps this schema to Group 3 fax capabilities.

The RFC defines capability identification as a form of capability exchange in which a receiving system tells a sending system what it can do, so the sender can pick a form of the data the receiver can use.
sections.eli5: A fax machine can say 'here is what I can print' using a shared list of words. The sender reads the list and picks a version of the page that works.

sections.title: Syntax and Matching
sections.content:
The schema does not invent its own syntax. Descriptions are written in the format of 'A syntax for describing media feature sets' (RFC 2533), which combines individual feature tags registered under the Media Feature Tag Registration Procedure (RFC 2506). The tags provide a base vocabulary, and the feature set syntax combines them into descriptions of whole combinations of capabilities.

Listing a tag does not mean a system must have that capability. A system must recognize the tag and deal with it according to the capabilities it does have, and it may offer additional tags. If a system receives an unrecognized or unused tag, the feature set matching rule makes it effectively ignored.
sections.eli5: Everyone uses the same grammar, like a form with fixed boxes. If you see a box you do not understand, you skip it and keep going.

sections.title: Size, Resolution, Media and Paper
sections.content:
The simplest tags describe the page. size-x and size-y give a rendered document size in inches, as positive rational numbers. A size measured in millimetres can be converted exactly with a factor of 10/254.

dpi is the resolution as a positive integer, and dpi-xyratio is a positive rational. If the ratio is present and not 1, dpi is the horizontal resolution and the vertical resolution is dpi divided by the ratio. For MRC documents, the complete set of usable resolutions is listed, with two restrictions: 100dpi can be used only with multi-level images, and any multi-level image resolution must be an integral sub-multiple of the applicable mask resolution.

ua-media describes the kind of medium: screen, screen-paged, stationery, transparency, envelope, envelope-plain or continuous. paper-size takes A4, A3, B4, letter or legal. The last two tags are defined in RFC 2534, and size-x, size-y and dpi-xyratio are registered in the appendix of this document.
sections.eli5: These words say how big the page is, how many tiny dots fit in an inch, and what the page is made of, like normal paper or a see-through sheet.

sections.title: Color Capability and Color Model
sections.content:
The color tag gives a broad indication of color handling: Binary (bi-level only), Limited (a limited number of colors), Mapped (palette or otherwise mapped color), Grey (grey-scale only) or Full (full continuous-tone color). In Internet fax, Limited is read as one bit per color sample. The value also hints at which finer tags apply.

Those finer tags follow a receiver's view of an image in stages: a raw bit stream is decoded into pixel values, mapped to color values, and then related to a physical rendition on a display or printer. Grey scale and bi-level images are a special case with a one-component color model, and tags that stand for an implied, unknown or don't-care value may simply be omitted.

color-levels gives the number of distinct values per picture element; for bi-level images 2 is implied. color-space is Device-RGB, Device-CMY, Device-CMYK or CIELAB. Device spaces are defined by the receiving device, while calibrated ones assume a calibrated rendering system. A calibrated space should be used when precise matching is needed and the receiver is not known. color-illuminant names a CIE illuminant using the Group 3 form, such as D50 (the Group 3 default) or CTnnnn for a color temperature in Kelvins. The CIELAB-L-depth, -a-depth and -b-depth tags count representable values per component, and the -min and -max tags give a color gamut.
sections.eli5: Some machines only know black and white, some know shades of grey, and some know every color. The color words say which kind a machine is, and extra words say exactly how it mixes its colors.

sections.title: Image Coding and MRC
sections.content:
Several tags say how image data is packed. image-file-structure says how coded data is wrapped: TIFF, TIFF-limited, TIFF-minimal (the minimal black and white mode, also known as TIFF-S), TIFF-MRC (the Mixed Raster Content structure, also known as TIFF-M) or TIFF-MRC-limited. image-coding says how the raw data is compressed: MH, MR, MMR, JBIG or JPEG. image-coding-constraint narrows this to a particular environment with JBIG-T85, JBIG-T43 or JPEG-T4E.

Other tags refine the choice: JBIG-stripe-size (number of scan lines per stripe, for example 128), image-interleave (Stripe or Plane) and color-subsampling ("1:1:1" or "4:1:1"). The RFC warns that the file structure alone does not describe a recipient. A general rule is to give enough detail to exclude anything unsupported, and for extended Internet fax to always specify both image-file-structure and image-coding.

For MRC, MRC-mode is an integer from 0 to 7: zero means MRC is not available and a non-zero value is the maximum available mode. An MRC document is several images, each described by its own feature collection. Foreground and background images use multi-level coders (odd layers) and mask layers use bi-level coders (even layers). MRC-max-stripe-size is an upper bound on scan lines per stripe, with legal constraints of at most 256 and at least 0.
sections.eli5: These words say how a picture is squished into a file and how the file is wrapped, like saying whether your picture is rolled in a tube or folded in an envelope. Some machines can also unpack pictures that are stacked in layers.

sections.title: Worked Capability Examples
sections.content:
Section 4 builds up a series of example capability descriptions: a simple mode Internet fax system (which must support TIFF profile S), a high-end black-and-white system with JBIG (similar to what is sometimes called 'Super G3'), a grey-scale system, two full-color systems (JPEG only, then JPEG and JBIG) and a full-color system with MRC. Each adds capabilities to the previous one, using the & (and) and | (or) operators.

The last example shows feature matching. A receiver describes an enhanced black-and-white system. The sender has the same document in three forms: A4 high resolution, B4 low resolution and A4 high resolution color. The forms are combined with a logical OR and matched against the receiver by the rules of RFC 2533. The color version is eliminated because the receiver cannot handle color or JPEG. The 300dpi version must use JBIG, the only coding that sender and receiver share for that resolution. The low-resolution B4 version can use either MH or MR. Even if the sender does not understand ua-media, the matching rules preserve the receiver's constraint on it. For an MRC document, each component sub-image must match the receiver's capabilities.
sections.eli5: The examples are like a menu and an order. The receiver lists what it can eat, the sender lists what it can cook, and matching them shows the dishes that work for both.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The points in this RFC add to the security considerations for extended Internet fax. The main concern is privacy: negotiation reveals information about one party to others, which might help a malicious party guess at specific security holes. This document specifies the capabilities, not how they are published. Implementers and users should make sure the mechanism used reveals capabilities only to appropriate persons, systems and agents.

One specific threat is listed: unsolicited bulk mail. If a recipient is known to process certain kinds of images, bulk mailers might target it with those images.
sections.eli5: If everyone knows exactly what your machine can do, a pest could use that to send you junk. So only tell the people who need to know.

sections.title: Registrations
sections.content: Appendix A repeats the feature tag descriptions introduced by RFC 2531, with small revisions, and registers them in the IETF tree under the Media Feature Tag Registration Procedure. These tags are therefore subject to the 'IETF Consensus' policy of RFC 2434. Appendix A.5 introduces one new tag, color-illuminant, to be registered the same way; an ASN.1 identifier should be assigned and filled into the registration.
sections.eli5: Each word on the list is officially written in a public book, so everyone agrees what it means. One new word was added in this version.

items.title: Raw bit stream
items.text: A stream of coded bits. Step A is image coding or decoding.

items.title: Pixel values
items.text: One number per picture element. Step B maps pixels to color values.

items.title: Color values
items.text: One number per color component, such as L*, a*, b*. Step C relates them to a physical color.

items.title: Physical rendition
items.text: A color value realized on a display, printer or other device.

items.label: Plain TIFF
items.desc: Image data enclosed and tagged with TIFF structures.

items.label: Limited IFD placement
items.desc: TIFF with the IFD placement limits of RFC 2301.

items.label: TIFF-S
items.desc: Minimal black and white mode of RFC 2301.

items.label: TIFF-M
items.desc: TIFF with a sub-IFD structure for Mixed Raster Content images.

items.label: MRC, limited primary IFDs
items.desc: Same as TIFF-MRC, with top-level IFD placement constrained like TIFF-limited.
